titulo.texto: MMAPO, the Morelos Museum of Folk Art

frase_gancho.texto: Life-size chinelos, pots from Cuentepec, textiles from Hueyapan, and figures from Tlayacapan, all steps from the palace.

puente_narrativo.texto: Walk along Hidalgo Street toward the Cathedral, if your route continues that way.

guion_corto.texto: On Hidalgo Street, number two hundred thirty-nine, there is a museum with part of its collection outdoors. It is the Morelos Museum of Folk Art, known as MMAPO. It shows crafts from all the regions of Morelos. There is ceramics from Cuentepec, textiles from Hueyapan, and work by artisans from Tlayacapan. Part of what it exhibits is outdoors, so you can get close to the pieces. Among them, the life-size chinelos stand out, the dancers of the Morelos carnival, with their long tunic and decorated hat. It is a museum that tells the story of the state through the hands that make objects of clay, wool, and other materials. Most of its pieces are for sale and change often.

guion_largo.texto:
The Cortés palace told you the history of Morelos through its stones and its murals. MMAPO tells it through the hands of the people who make objects every day. The entrance is on Hidalgo Street, number two hundred thirty-nine, between the palace and the Cathedral.

The full name is the Morelos Museum of Folk Art, and those who know it call it MMAPO. It brings together crafts from all the regions of the state. The idea is to preserve, exhibit, and promote the work of the artisans of Morelos, and to help keep that craft alive.

Three communities come up whenever people talk about Morelos crafts. The first is Cuentepec, known for its women potters, who work with clay. The second is Hueyapan, where wool is woven: you already saw its skeins in the palace museum. The third is Tlayacapan, whose craftwork is also shown in the museum. Tlayacapan also appears in an exhibit in the palace about spindle whorls, the weights on a spindle used for spinning thread since pre-Hispanic times.

The most eye-catching figures at MMAPO are the chinelos. They are the dancers of the Morelos carnival, and the museum shows them life-size. They wear a long tunic, a mask with a beard, and a tall hat with decorations. When they dance, they take short hops to the rhythm of a band. The museum lets you get close to them and see how they are made, detail by detail.

According to tradition, the chinelo was born in the nineteenth century as a mockery by villagers of the hacienda owners, which is why its attire exaggerates the elegance of the landowners. It is an explanation that is often repeated, although the origins of the dance are still debated. What is clear is that today it is a symbol of the state and that every carnival fills it again with music and color.

One feature of MMAPO is that many objects are outdoors. That changes the experience. Instead of closed display cases, you can see the pieces up close, in daylight.

There is also a shop. The pieces change often and almost all are for sale, so what you see today may not be there tomorrow. If you buy something, ask the person helping you where it comes from and who made it. In folk art, the name of the person and of the town matter as much as the object.

Before going in, pause on the street. This museum sits between the cathedral and the Cortés Palace, so it serves as a rest between two big stops. Here the pace changes: fewer dates and more objects that you can take in with your eyes, one by one.

This museum is the living side of Morelos: the objects are not just the past, they are made and sold today.

The word folk has a precise meaning. It does not mean cheap or simple. It means made by the people, with techniques passed down from generation to generation. Between Rivera’s mural and a pot from Cuentepec there is more of a connection than it seems: both tell the story of Morelos.

texto: Look for the life-size chinelos and notice the tunic, the beard, and the hat
Find a clay piece and a wool piece and guess which town each one comes from
Ask in the shop who made the piece that catches your eye and where they live

texto.Collection: crafts from all the regions of Morelos

texto.pregunta: Myth: Folk art is the same as cheap crafts from the market.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is handmade work using techniques that are inherited. MMAPO presents it as art, with the name of its community.
